Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Overview Framework Combine Customize handling of asynchronous events by combining event- processing operators. iOS 13.0+ iPadOS 13.0+ Mac Catalyst 13.0+macOS 10.15+ tvOS 13.0+ visionOS 1.0+ watchOS 6.0+

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.
Routing Notifications to Combine Subscribers Deliver notifications to subscribers by using notification centersʼ publishers.

query_processing.original_query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

query_processing.original_query: What does the Combine framework provide?

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Overview Framework Combine Customize handling of asynchronous events by combining event- processing operators. iOS 13.0+ iPadOS 13.0+ Mac Catalyst 13.0+macOS 10.15+ tvOS 13.0+ visionOS 1.0+ watchOS 6.0+

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

data.query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

query_processing.original_query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

chunks.content: ## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} Returns build attestations for a subject digest. Each attestation includes a `bundle` property containing the full attestation bundle inline: ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle": { "mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle+json;version=0.3", "verificationMaterial": {} } }] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number} The singular **`assignee` field has been removed.** Use the `assignees` array instead. ```json { "number": 10, "assignees": [{ "login": "octocat" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** read and write assignees exclusively through the `assignees` array.

query: On the current API version, what status code does deleting a GitHub App installation return?

data.query: On the current API version, what status code does deleting a GitHub App installation return?

query_processing.original_query: On the current API version, what status code does deleting a GitHub App installation return?

chunks.content: ## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} Removes a GitHub App installation. On success, returns **`204 No Content`**.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path} Submodule entries now correctly report **`"type": "submodule"`** instead of `"type": "file"`: ```json { "name": "vendor/lib", "type": "submodule", "submodule_git_url": "https://github.com/example/lib.git" } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** any code that branched on `type === "file"` to detect regular files must now also exclude `"submodule"` explicitly, since submodules no longer masquerade as files.

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Overview Framework Combine Customize handling of asynchronous events by combining event- processing operators. iOS 13.0+ iPadOS 13.0+ Mac Catalyst 13.0+macOS 10.15+ tvOS 13.0+ visionOS 1.0+ watchOS 6.0+

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

data.query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

query_processing.original_query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

chunks.content: ## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} Returns build attestations for a subject digest. Each attestation includes a `bundle` property containing the full attestation bundle inline: ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle": { "mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle+json;version=0.3", "verificationMaterial": {} } }] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number} The singular **`assignee` field has been removed.** Use the `assignees` array instead. ```json { "number": 10, "assignees": [{ "login": "octocat" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** read and write assignees exclusively through the `assignees` array.

query_processing.original_query: On the current API version, what status code does deleting a GitHub App installation return?

query_processing.original_query: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

query_processing.original_query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

chunks.content: ## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} Returns build attestations for a subject digest. Each attestation includes a `bundle` property containing the full attestation bundle inline: ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle": { "mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle+json;version=0.3", "verificationMaterial": {} } }] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number} The singular **`assignee` field has been removed.** Use the `assignees` array instead. ```json { "number": 10, "assignees": [{ "login": "octocat" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** read and write assignees exclusively through the `assignees` array.

query: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

data.query: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

query_processing.original_query: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

Convenience Publishers Connectable Publishers Subscribers protocol Subscriber A protocol that declares a type that can receive input from a publisher. enum Subscribers A namespace for types that serve as subscribers. struct AnySubscriber A type-erasing subscriber. protocol Subscription A protocol representing the connection of a subscriber to a publisher. enum Subscriptions A namespace for symbols related to subscriptions.

query_processing.original_query: What does the Combine framework provide?

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

chunks.content: ## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/default-setup Returns the default setup configuration for code scanning. The `languages` array may contain `javascript` and `typescript` as **separate** values: ```json { "state": "configured", "languages": ["javascript", "typescript", "python"] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/default-setup The `languages` array no longer contains `javascript` and `typescript` as separate values — they are combined into a single **`javascript-typescript`** value, since CodeQL analyzes them together. ```json { "state": "configured", "languages": ["javascript-typescript", "python"] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** replace checks for `"javascript"` or `"typescript"` individually with a check for `"javascript-typescript"`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} Returns build attestations for a subject digest. Each attestation includes a `bundle` property containing the full attestation bundle inline: ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle": { "mediaType": "application/vnd.dev.sigstore.bundle+json;version=0.3", "verificationMaterial": {} } }] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path} Submodule entries now correctly report **`"type": "submodule"`** instead of `"type": "file"`: ```json { "name": "vendor/lib", "type": "submodule", "submodule_git_url": "https://github.com/example/lib.git" } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** any code that branched on `type === "file"` to detect regular files must now also exclude `"submodule"` explicitly, since submodules no longer masquerade as files.

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

The `languages` array may contain `javascript` and `typescript` as **separate** values: ```json { "state": "configured", "languages": ["javascript", "typescript", "python"] } ```

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/default-setup The `languages` array no longer contains `javascript` and `typescript` as separate values — they are combined into a single **`javascript-typescript`** value, since CodeQL analyzes them together. ```json { "state": "configured", "languages": ["javascript-typescript", "python"] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** replace checks for `"javascript"` or `"typescript"` individually with a check for `"javascript-typescript"`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

chunks.content: Convenience Publishers Connectable Publishers Subscribers protocol Subscriber A protocol that declares a type that can receive input from a publisher. enum Subscribers A namespace for types that serve as subscribers. struct AnySubscriber A type-erasing subscriber. protocol Subscription A protocol representing the connection of a subscriber to a publisher. enum Subscriptions A namespace for symbols related to subscriptions.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

Subscriptions A namespace for symbols related to subscriptions. protocol Subject A publisher that exposes a method for outside callers to publish elements. class CurrentValueSubject A subject that wraps a single value and publishes a new element whenever the value changes. class PassthroughSubject A subject that broadcasts elements to downstream subscribers. protocol Scheduler A protocol that defines when and how to execute a closure. struct ImmediateScheduler A scheduler for performing synchronous actions.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Documentation Language:Swift use them to update your app. By adopting Combine, youʼll make your code easier to read and maintain, by centralizing your event-processing code and eliminating troublesome techniques like nested closures and convention-based callbacks.

This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.content: ## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} Removes a GitHub App installation. On success, returns **`204 No Content`**.

# GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /rate_limit Returns your current rate limit status. The response body includes a **top-level `rate` object** (deprecated, but still present in this version) in addition to `resources.core`: ```json { "resources": { "core": { "limit": 5000, "remaining": 4999, "reset": 1730000000 } }, "rate": { "limit": 5000, "remaining": 4999, "reset": 1730000000 } } ```

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

data.query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

query_processing.original_query: What changed about attestation list responses between API Version 2022-11-28 and 2026-03-10?

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.content: # GitHub REST API Reference — current-version **API Version:** `2026-03-10` Send this version via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2026-03-10` request header. This is the first API version to ship breaking changes since GitHub introduced calendar-versioned APIs. `2022-11-28` remains fully supported until at least 2028-03-10, and requests that omit the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header still default to `2022-11-28`, **not** to this version — you must opt in explicitly to get the changes below.

## GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/attestations/{subject_digest} The **`bundle` property has been removed** from attestation list responses. Use **`bundle_url`** to retrieve the attestation bundle instead. ```json { "attestations": [{ "bundle_url": "https://api.github.com/repos/example/example/attestations/download/sha256:abc123" }] } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** fetch the bundle from `bundle_url` rather than reading it inline from `bundle`.

# GitHub REST API Reference — old-version **API Version:** `2022-11-28` Send this version explicitly via the `X-GitHub-Api-Version: 2022-11-28` request header, or omit the header entirely — `2022-11-28` is the default version GitHub uses when no header is sent. It remains fully supported for at least 24 months after any newer version ships. This reference documents endpoint behavior as of API Version 2022-11-28, the version most existing integrations were built against before the 2026-03-10 breaking-changes release.

## DELETE /app/installations/{installation_id} This endpoint now returns **`202 Accepted`** instead of `204 No Content`; the deletion is processed in the background. > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** treat `202` as success, not just `204` — the installation may not be fully removed the instant the response is received.

## POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/workflows/{workflow_id}/dispatches The **`return_run_details` parameter has been removed.** On success, this endpoint now always returns **`200 OK`** with the triggered workflow run's details in the response body (previously `204 No Content` with no body). ```json { "id": 123456, "status": "queued", "workflow_id": 1 } ``` > **Migrating from 2022-11-28:** stop passing `return_run_details`, and update any code that expected `204 No Content` to instead parse the `200 OK` response body.

chunks.section: Receiving and Handling Events with Combine
chunks.content: Receiving and Handling Events with Combine Customize and receive events from asynchronous sources. protocol Publisher Declares that a type can transmit a sequence of values over time. enum Publishers A namespace for types that serve as publishers. struct AnyPublisher A publisher that performs type erasure by wrapping another publisher. struct Published A type that publishes a property marked with an attribute. protocol Cancellable A protocol indicating that an activity or action supports cancellation.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

Controlling Publishing with Connectable Publishers Coordinate when publishers start sending elements to subscribers. protocol ConnectablePublisher A publisher that provides an explicit means of connecting and canceling publication.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

chunks.section: Receiving and Handling Events with Combine
chunks.content: Receiving and Handling Events with Combine Customize and receive events from asynchronous sources. protocol Publisher Declares that a type can transmit a sequence of values over time. enum Publishers A namespace for types that serve as publishers. struct AnyPublisher A publisher that performs type erasure by wrapping another publisher. struct Published A type that publishes a property marked with an attribute. protocol Cancellable A protocol indicating that an activity or action supports cancellation.

chunks.section: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code
chunks.content: Using Combine for Your Appʼs Asynchronous Code Apply common patterns to migrate your closure-based, event-handling code. protocol ObservableObject A type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed. class ObservableObjectPublisher A publisher that publishes changes from observable objects. struct AsyncPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence. struct AsyncThrowingPublisher A publisher that exposes its elements as a throwing asynchronous sequence.

Controlling Publishing with Connectable Publishers Coordinate when publishers start sending elements to subscribers. protocol ConnectablePublisher A publisher that provides an explicit means of connecting and canceling publication.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

chunks.content: The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers and republish them. At the end of a chain of publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them.

f publishers, a Subscriber acts on elements as it receives them. Publishers only emit values when explicitly requested to do so by subscribers. This puts your subscriber code in control of how fast it receives events from the publishers itʼs connected to. Several Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers, including Timer, NotificationCenter, and URLSession. Combine also provides a built-in publisher for any property thatʼs compliant with Key-Value Observing.

To p i c s Essentials Publishers class Future A publisher that eventually produces a single value and then finishes or fails. struct Just A publisher that emits an output to each subscriber just once, and then finishes. struct Deferred A publisher that awaits subscription before running the supplied closure to create a publisher for the new subscriber. struct Empty A publisher that never publishes any values, and optionally finishes immediately. struct Fail A publisher that immediately terminates with the specified error. struct Record A publisher that allows for recording a series of inputs and a completion, for later playback to each subscriber.

- Users browse listings and can “like” items anonymously.  
- When two users **mutually like** each other’s listings, they become **swap candidates**.

prompt.user: tell me about the candidate ?

llm.answer:
The context describes **swap candidates** as part of the app’s anonymous swapping feature.  

- Users list items and can anonymously “like” other users’ listings.  
- When two users mutually like each other’s listings, the system creates a **swap candidate** for them.  
- The identities of the users remain hidden until the listing period ends, at which point the candidates can be revealed and the swap can proceed.  

So, a “candidate” here is a potential swap partner that is generated when both parties express interest in each other’s items.

prompt.user: How would system notifications be delivered to subscribers instead of using NotificationCenter's traditional observer API directly?

llm.answer:
System notifications can be delivered to subscribers through push‑notification services rather than by posting directly to NotificationCenter.  

In the projects described, the notifications are sent via **Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM)** for Android and **Apple Push Notification Service (APNs)** for iOS. These services handle delivery to the device whether the app is in the foreground, background, or even terminated, allowing the app to receive the notification through the platform’s push‑notification infrastructure instead of using NotificationCenter’s observer pattern.  

**Key points from the context**

* Implemented push‑notification workflows using **FCM and APNs** for all app states (foreground, background, terminated)【source id="2】.  
* The same approach was used for specific use‑cases such as warranty reminders, maintenance alerts, and user‑engagement updates【source id="3】.  
* Support for both Android and iOS platforms was provided through these push services【source id="4】.  

Thus, by leveraging FCM and APNs, system notifications are routed to subscribers through the respective cloud‑messaging services rather than relying on NotificationCenter’s traditional observer API.

llm.answer:
The app refers to **candidates** as the other users that appear on a leaderboard for a swap.  

- **Swap candidates** are the people a user can match with when they want to exchange listings.  
- By default only the top‑ranked candidates are available, but **users can pay to unlock additional swap candidates that are lower down the leaderboard**【Source 3】.  
- The **priority‑based swap decision** rule gives the user who listed first the first right to finalize a swap with a candidate from their leaderboard, ensuring a fair and structured match‑resolution process【Source 2】.

chunks.content:
The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares
publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over
time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

prompt.user: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

llm.answer: You can bridge a Combine publisher to Swift’s async/await model by using the **AsyncPublisher** (or **AsyncThrowingPublisher**) types that expose the publisher’s elements as an asynchronous sequence. Once you have an `AsyncPublisher`, you can consume its emitted values with a `for‑await` loop or other async‑sequence APIs instead of implementing a Combine `Subscriber` [Source 4].

Customize and receive events from asynchronous sources. protocol Publisher
Declares that a type can transmit a sequence of values over time.

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares
publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over
time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over

prompt.user: How can property changes tracked through Objective-C's Key-Value Observing mechanism be turned into a stream of values?

llm.answer: Combine provides a built‑in publisher that can observe any property that conforms to Objective‑C’s Key‑Value Observing (KVO) mechanism. By using this KVO publisher, the changes to the property are emitted as a stream of values that can be subscribed to and processed with Combine operators【Source 1】. This lets you expose KVO changes as a Combine publisher and treat them like any other asynchronous value stream【Source 3】.

prompt.user: How can values be emitted at regular time intervals without writing a raw timer callback yourself?

llm.answer: You can use Combine’s built‑in timer publisher, which emits elements on a regular schedule so you don’t need to write a raw timer callback yourself. The framework provides a timer publisher that “publish[es] elements periodically by using a timer” and replaces the need for a manual Foundation Timer callback【Source 3】. Additionally, Foundation’s Timer type is exposed as a Combine publisher, allowing you to receive timed values directly through the publisher‑subscriber chain【Source 1】.

prompt.user: How can a publisher's emitted values be consumed using Swift's async/await syntax instead of its own subscriber APIs?

llm.answer: You can convert a Combine publisher to an asynchronous sequence by using the **`AsyncPublisher`** type. `AsyncPublisher` “exposes its elements as an asynchronous sequence,” which lets you consume the emitted values with Swift’s `async/await` syntax (e.g., `for await value in publisher.values { … }`) instead of implementing a traditional `Subscriber` [Source 4].

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares
publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over
time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

llm.answer: You can turn a Combine publisher into an asynchronous sequence by using the `AsyncPublisher` (or `AsyncThrowingPublisher`) types. These publishers expose their emitted elements as an async sequence, which lets you consume the values with Swift’s `async/await` syntax—e.g., using a `for‑await` loop—rather than implementing a Combine subscriber yourself【Source 4】.

llm.answer: System notifications can be routed to Combine subscribers by using NotificationCenter’s Combine publisher instead of adding observers manually. The publisher emits notification events, which subscribers can receive through the normal Combine subscription chain【Source 1】.

prompt.user: How can property changes tracked through Objective-C's Key-Value Observing mechanism be turned into a stream of values?

llm.answer: You can use Combine’s built‑in KVO publisher – any property that is KVO‑compliant can be exposed as a Combine publisher, which turns each KVO change into a streamed value for subscribers【Source 1】. This “Expose KVO changes with a Combine publisher” pattern lets property updates be emitted as a continuous stream of values【Source 2】.

publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those

time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

prompt.user: What are the benefits of adopting Combine in your code?

llm.answer:
Adopting Combine can:

* Make your code **easier to read and maintain** by centralising event‑processing logic and removing “troublesome” patterns such as nested closures and convention‑based callbacks【Source 1】.  
* Give you a **declarative Swift API** for handling values that arrive over time, simplifying asynchronous code【Source 4】.  
* Put the **subscriber in control of the event flow**, because publishers only emit when explicitly requested, allowing you to manage how fast events are received【Source 5】.

chunks.content:
The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares
publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over
time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

prompt.user: How does Combine uniquely identify publisher streams for debugging?

llm.answer: Combine gives each publisher stream a unique identifier through the **`CombineIdentifier`** type. Publishers (or other stream‑related types) can conform to the **`CustomCombineIdentifierConvertible`** protocol, which supplies this identifier, allowing developers to distinguish and debug individual streams. [Source 1]

The Combine framework provides a declarative Swift API for processing values over time. These values can represent many kinds of asynchronous events. Combine declares
publishers to expose values that can change over time, and subscribers to receive those
values from the publishers. The Publisher protocol declares a type that can deliver a sequence of values over
time. Publishers have operators to act on the values received from upstream publishers
and republish them.

prompt.user: How does Combine replace closure-based asynchronous event handling?

llm.answer: Combine replaces closure‑based asynchronous event handling by providing a unified publisher/subscriber model that centralizes event processing and removes the need for nested closures or convention‑based callbacks. By adopting Combine you can migrate closure‑based code to declarative streams, making the code easier to read and maintain【Source 2】. The framework includes patterns and types (e.g., Publisher, ObservableObject, AsyncPublisher) specifically designed to move away from manual closure handling toward reactive pipelines【Source 1】【Source 3】.

prompt.user: What is the difference between Empty and Fail publishers?

llm.answer:
**Empty** publishers never emit any values; they may simply finish without emitting anything (or finish immediately) [Source 1].

**Fail** publishers, by contrast, terminate right away by sending a specified error to the subscriber [Source 2].

So, the key difference is that **Empty** produces no values and can finish normally, whereas **Fail** ends the stream with an error as soon as it is subscribed to.

prompt.user: What is the difference between TopLevelEncoder and TopLevelDecoder?

llm.answer:
TopLevelEncoder and TopLevelDecoder are separate protocols that serve opposite purposes:

- **TopLevelEncoder** is a protocol that defines methods for **encoding** data — converting Swift values into an external representation such as JSON or Property List. [Source 1]  
- **TopLevelDecoder** is a protocol that defines methods for **decoding** data — converting an external representation back into Swift values. [Source 1]

prompt.user: How does Combine replace closure-based asynchronous event handling?

llm.answer: Combine replaces closure‑based asynchronous event handling by introducing a declarative, publisher‑subscriber model. Instead of passing nested callbacks or other closure‑based techniques to receive events, you expose values through **publishers** and let **subscribers** receive those values. This centralizes event‑processing code, removes the need for convention‑based callbacks and nested closures, and lets you migrate existing closure‑based code to a more readable, maintainable pattern [Source 1][Source 2]. The framework’s core concepts—publishers that emit a sequence of values over time and subscribers that handle those values—provide the underlying mechanism that replaces the traditional closure approach [Source 3].

prompt.user: What is the difference between CurrentValueSubject and PassthroughSubject?

llm.answer:
CurrentValueSubject and PassthroughSubject are both Combine subjects, but they behave differently:

* **PassthroughSubject** simply broadcasts each element it receives to its downstream subscribers without retaining any state. It does not keep a “current” value — subscribers only see values that are sent after they subscribe【Source 1】.  

* **CurrentValueSubject** holds a single, current value. When that value changes, it publishes the new element, and new subscribers immediately receive the latest stored value upon subscription【Source 1】【Source 2】.  

In short, PassthroughSubject is a fire‑and‑forget broadcaster, while CurrentValueSubject is a stateful subject that always retains and emits its most recent value.

prompt.user: What is the difference between Empty and Fail publishers?

llm.answer:
**Empty publisher** – It never emits any values to its subscribers. It can optionally finish immediately with a normal completion, but it does not produce data. [Source 1]

**Fail publisher** – It terminates right away by sending a failure completion that contains a specified error. [Source 1]

Thus, the key difference is that **Empty** completes without emitting values (and without an error), whereas **Fail** completes with an error as soon as it is subscribed to.

llm.answer:

prompt.user: What are publishers and subscribers in Combine?

llm.answer:
In Combine, **publishers** are objects that emit a stream of values (or events) over time. Many Foundation types expose their functionality through publishers—for example Timer, NotificationCenter, URLSession, and any KVO‑compliant property—and you can combine the output of multiple publishers to drive further processing [Source 1].

**Subscribers** are the counterpart that receive those values. A subscriber conforms to the `Subscriber` protocol, which declares a type that can receive input from a publisher. The framework also provides a namespace (`Subscribers`) and type‑erasing wrappers such as `AnySubscriber` for implementing or using subscribers [Source 2].

Together, publishers produce elements and subscribers consume them, enabling reactive data flow in Combine.

llm.answer:
**ObservableObject** is a protocol that represents “a type of object with a publisher that emits before the object has changed.” It supplies a publisher so that subscribers can be notified just prior to any change in the object’s state【Source 2】.  

**ObservableObjectPublisher** is a class that serves as “a publisher that publishes changes from observable objects.” It delivers the change notifications generated by objects conforming to ObservableObject to any subscribers【Source 1】.

prompt.user: What is the difference between CurrentValueSubject and PassthroughSubject?

llm.answer:
CurrentValueSubject and PassthroughSubject are both Combine subjects, but they behave differently:

* **CurrentValueSubject** wraps a single stored value and automatically publishes a new element whenever that value changes. It retains the latest value and can deliver it to new subscribers. [Source 2]

* **PassthroughSubject** simply broadcasts elements that are sent to it; it does not store a current value or replay the latest element to new subscribers. [Source 1]
